> This guide is the English version of
> [7. Del hallazgo a la métrica](del-hallazgo-a-la-metrica.html). `lupa` writes
> its messages and tables in Spanish, so the output below is in Spanish.

The profile of `datos_operativos` says that the column `canal` (*channel*) has
missing values. They are disguised: one is `"S/D"` and another, an empty text.
How does that finding become a measurement that repeats with each delivery and
is compared with a requirement?

> **In this guide:**
>
> - going from the findings to a proposal of metrics with `proponer_modelo()`;
> - deciding what is measured and measuring it with `medir()`;
> - aggregating the measures of each cell up to the column with `agregar()`;
> - evaluating the aggregated measure against a threshold with `evaluar()`;
> - seeing which part of a quality framework was covered with
>   `cobertura_analisis()`.

## The starting finding

The table is profiled and the findings of the profile in `canal` are inspected.
The date is fixed so that the example always gives the same result.

```{r}
library(lupa)

perfil <- perfilar(datos_operativos, fecha = "2026-01-15")
encontrados <- hallazgos(perfil)
encontrados[encontrados$columna %in% "canal", c("tipo_hallazgo", "severidad")]
```

The one with severity `error` is `faltantes_disfrazados` (*disguised missing
values*). Its evidence says which ones they are:

```{r}
disfrazados <- encontrados$columna %in% "canal" &
  encontrados$tipo_hallazgo == "faltantes_disfrazados"
writeLines(encontrados$evidencia[disfrazados])
```

A finding describes this delivery. To know whether the next one is better or
worse, and whether it reaches the required level, a metric is needed.

## From the findings to a proposal of metrics

A metric is a named way of measuring. It is bound to a table and to one or more
columns, and it returns a result for each object it measures. `NoNulo` (*not
null*), the completeness metric, returns a 1 for each cell with a value and a 0
for each empty cell. What counts as empty is part of its configuration: besides
`NA`, the values declared to it in `valores_nulos` (*null values*).

`lupa` does not decide what to measure: it proposes. `proponer_modelo()`
(*propose a model*) goes through the findings and returns an editable table,
with one row per suggested metric and the finding it came from. It measures
nothing.

```{r}
propuesta <- proponer_modelo(perfil, datos_operativos)
propuesta[, c("metrica", "atributos", "origen", "incluir")]
```

The column `incluir` (*include*) says which rows stay active. `lupa` marks them
like this:

- it activates the ones that come from an observed defect: the missing values
  of `r sum(propuesta$metrica == "NoNulo" & propuesta$incluir)` columns and the
  duplicated rows;
- it leaves off the ones that come from a habit of this delivery, such as a
  format pattern or the domain of `zona` (*zone*).

A single delivery does not show that those habits are requirements. And
measuring them on the same delivery they came from would say little.

The row of `canal` shows the step from the finding to the metric. The values
that the profile recognized as disguised missing values move into the
configuration of `NoNulo`:

```{r}
fila_canal <- which(propuesta$id_sugerencia == "NoNulo:canal")
writeLines(strwrap(propuesta$justificacion[fila_canal], 88))
propuesta$configuracion[[fila_canal]]
```

## Deciding what is measured

The proposal is edited: the decision belongs to whoever uses it. Here the
interest is completeness: only the
`r sum(propuesta$metrica == "NoNulo")` rows of `NoNulo` stay active, and the
one for duplicates is turned off. `modelo_desde_propuesta()` (*model from
proposal*) turns the active rows into an operational model. It is the list of
metrics, already bound to their columns, that `medir()` (*measure*) is going to
run. It does not measure either.

```{r}
propuesta$incluir <- propuesta$metrica == "NoNulo"
propuesta[propuesta$incluir, c("metrica", "atributos")]
modelo_completitud <- modelo_desde_propuesta(propuesta)
```

## Measuring

`medir()` takes the model first and the data after. The identifier and the date
of the run stay in each measure; with them, deliveries are compared later.

```{r}
medicion <- medir(
  modelo_completitud, datos_operativos,
  id_medicion = "entrega-enero",
  fecha = "2026-01-15"
)
nrow(medicion)
medicion[medicion$atributo == "canal", c("objeto_medible", "resultado")]
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(
  medicion$fila[medicion$atributo == "canal" & medicion$resultado == 0],
  c(5L, 13L)
))
```

Each row is a measure: a result for an object, here a cell. The
`r length(unique(medicion$atributo))` columns by `r nrow(datos_operativos)`
rows give `r nrow(medicion)` measures. In `canal`, rows 5 and 13 are 0. They
are the `"S/D"` and the empty text, which `NoNulo` counted as missing because
the configuration asked it to.

## Aggregating up to the column

One measure per cell does not yet answer the underlying question: how complete
each column is. For that, the measures are aggregated. The vocabulary of the
levels is the one of the quality framework, and `granularidades()`
(*granularities*) translates it into the one of tables:

```{r}
granularidades()[c(1, 2, 4, 5), c("granularidad", "relacional")]
```

In a table:

- an attribute instance is a cell;
- an attribute, a column;
- an entity instance, a row (a tuple);
- an entity, a table.

These terms are also in [the glossary](leer-un-perfil.html#glosario) (in
Spanish). From the cell to the column the step is `ratio`, which computes the
proportion of ones:

```{r}
completitud <- agregar(medicion, "atributo", "ratio")
completitud[, c("atributo", "resultado", "agregacion")]
```

`agregar()` (*aggregate*) combines measures of a single metric and a single run.
It only follows the steps that `transiciones_granularidad()` (*granularity
transitions*) declares:

- from the cell to the column or to the row;
- from the column or the row to the table;
- from the table upwards.

A cell can be aggregated towards its column or towards its row: they are 2
different directions, not rungs of a single ladder. The available aggregations
are:

- `ratio`, for boolean results;
- `ratio_umbral` (*threshold ratio*), for real results compared with a
  threshold;
- `promedio` (*mean*);
- `promedio_ponderado` (*weighted mean*), with weights in `[0, 1]` that add up
  to 1 per target.

Unbounded results keep their unit and do not enter these aggregations. They are,
for example, the deviation of `ErrorEstandar` (*standard error*) or a staleness
measured in days.

## Evaluating against a threshold

A rule expresses a condition on results. An evaluation profile gathers rules.
That profile is not the object `perfilar()` returns: it is the second argument
of `evaluar()` (*evaluate*). Each column is required to be at least 90%
complete:

```{r}
regla <- regla_evaluacion(
  "Completitud de al menos 90 %",
  function(x) x >= 0.9
)
publicable <- perfil_evaluacion("Publicable", regla)
evaluacion <- evaluar(completitud, publicable)
evaluacion$perfiles[, c("perfil", "n_reglas", "resultado")]
```

The rule was applied to each of the `r nrow(completitud)` aggregated measures.
The result of a rule is the proportion of measures that meet it. The result of
a profile is the simple mean of its rules. These are the ones that met it:

```{r}
cumple <- evaluacion$medidas$resultado[
  match(completitud$id_medida, evaluacion$medidas$id_medida)
]
data.frame(
  columna = completitud$atributo,
  completitud = round(completitud$resultado, 3),
  cumple = cumple
)
```

Every column reaches 90% except `canal`, which has
`r round(completitud$resultado[completitud$atributo == "canal"], 3)`: the
result is `r sum(cumple)` out of `r length(cumple)`. The rule really compares
the completeness of each column with its threshold. Another threshold gives
another result:

```{r}
resultado_con_umbral <- function(umbral, medidas) {
  regla <- regla_evaluacion("Completitud", function(x) x >= umbral)
  evaluar(medidas, perfil_evaluacion("Publicable", regla))$perfiles$resultado
}
umbrales <- c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95)
data.frame(
  umbral = umbrales,
  agregada = vapply(umbrales, resultado_con_umbral, numeric(1), completitud),
  por_celda = vapply(umbrales, resultado_con_umbral, numeric(1), medicion)
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# What the text states about this table.
stopifnot(
  identical(
    vapply(umbrales, resultado_con_umbral, numeric(1), completitud),
    c(1, 0.75, 0)
  ),
  length(unique(vapply(umbrales, resultado_con_umbral, numeric(1), medicion))) == 1L
)
cumplen_por_umbral <- round(
  vapply(umbrales, resultado_con_umbral, numeric(1), completitud) * nrow(completitud)
)
```

With the aggregated measure, the result follows the threshold:

- with 80%, all `r cumplen_por_umbral[[1]]` columns meet it;
- with 90%, `r cumplen_por_umbral[[2]]` meet it;
- with 95%, none.

The column `por_celda` (*per cell*) shows what happens if the measurement is
evaluated without aggregating. The rule asks each cell whether its 0 or its 1
reaches the threshold. The result is the proportion of cells with a value,
`r round(mean(medicion$resultado), 3)`, whatever the threshold. That is why the
measures are aggregated before evaluating.

The evaluation applies a condition to measures that already exist. It does not
read `datos_operativos` again or replace the measurement.

## 🔎 What was covered {#what-was-covered}

The absence of findings does not prove that a table is fine: maybe nobody
measured what matters. `cobertura_analisis()` (*analysis coverage*) crosses the
profile and the measurement with a quality framework. It says, factor by
factor, what was measured. The third argument is called `modelo` (*model*), but
it takes a framework such as the one `marco_calidad()` (*quality framework*)
creates. By default, the AGESIC one.

```{r}
cobertura <- cobertura_analisis(perfil, medicion, modelo = marco_agesic())
cobertura[, c("dimension", "factor", "estado")]
```

`estado` (*status*) tells these cases apart:

- `medida` (*measured*);
- `no_declarada` (*not declared*), when nobody asked to measure it;
- `no_aplica` (*does not apply*), when it does not fit the types of the table,
  like positional accuracy when there are no geometries;
- `fuera_de_alcance` (*out of scope*), when `lupa` cannot measure it and says
  so.

Each row explains why:

```{r}
medidos <- cobertura[cobertura$estado == "medida", ]
writeLines(paste0(medidos$factor, ": ", medidos$motivo))
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(as.character(medidos$factor), c("Densidad", "No-duplicaci\u00f3n")))
```

Density was backed by the measurement; non-duplication, by what the profile
examines on its own. What is missing carries how to solve it:

```{r}
sintaxis <- cobertura$factor == "Correctitud sintáctica"
writeLines(cobertura$como_resolverlo[sintaxis])
```

## Summary

- `proponer_modelo()` turns the findings into an editable proposal: the
  disguised missing values the profile found move into the configuration of
  `NoNulo`.
- The column `incluir` is decided by whoever uses the proposal; what was
  learned from a single delivery arrives turned off.
- `medir()` returns one measure per object, with the `id_medicion` and the date
  of the run.
- Aggregate before evaluating: `agregar(medicion, "atributo", "ratio")` gives
  the completeness of each column, and the rule compares that number with its
  threshold.
- `cobertura_analisis()` says which factors of the framework were measured and
  how to cover the missing ones.
